## Welcome

I am a PhD candidate in Applied Economics at Oregon State University, on the
2026–27 economics job market. Prior to joining Oregon State, I earned my M.S. in
Economics and my B.S. in Business and Economic Analytics from Boise State
University. I also teach Principles of Microeconomics and Macroeconomics as
part-time faculty at Linn-Benton Community College.

As an applied microeconomist, I study the economics of wildfire, forest
management, and climate change adaptation. My research asks how a changing fire
regime reshapes the decisions of private forest owners, drawing on spatial and
panel data methods to connect environmental risk to land use and management
across the western United States.

My job market paper provides the first large-scale evidence that private forest
landowners are adapting to intensifying wildfire risk through forest management
practices. Linking confidential plot-level forest inventory data with wildfire
perimeters and fire-season weather, I find that increases in wildfire risk
perceptions cause landowners to harvest more and plant at lower densities,
reducing standing volume in non-federal western forests by roughly 7 to 10
percent. This adaptation generates numerous social benefits and social costs.
For the 2020 wildfire season, we find that landowner adaptation led to increases
in wildfire PM2.5 and reductions in wildfire carbon emissions. We estimate
damages of increased PM2.5 at \$63-\$72 million, outweighing climate benefits
of \$28-\$58 million.

**Job market paper:** [Landowner Expectations of Wildfire Risk have Accelerated
Harvest and Reduced Volume in Western U.S. Forests](research.qmd) &nbsp;[PDF](papers/jmp.pdf){.btn .btn-outline-primary .btn-sm}
